Explanation

Your application has hardcoded URLs that might correspond to services that are not accessible on Azure.

Review and ensure that the application is attempting to access URLs that would be available from Azure. You might need to migrate those services to Azure too, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.

If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premises, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
SQL database connection detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

SQL database connection detected.

Ensure the database is available/reachable on Azure.

If it is not, there are multiple ways you can move your data to Azure:
1. Migrate to Azure SQL Database.
2. Consider Azure SQL Managed Instance if you need features that are not available in Azure SQL Database and you don’t want to use a VM.
3. Migrate your database servers directly to SQL Server on Azure VMs.

To assess database migration effort, you can use Azure Migrate tool, see the link below.
Local or network IO operations detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 57

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.csLine 56

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj
src\eShopWinForms\eShopWinForms.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.
Connection strings without configuration builders detected
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

Connection strings without configuration builders detected.

Keeping connection strings directly in the app is not the best practice and might introduce security risks, increased maintenance, scalability challenges or compliance standards (such as PCI DSS, GDPR, etc.).

Instead, it is recommended to use configuration builders to get secrets from secure sources in Azure environment.
System.Data.SqlClient dependency detected
 Optional 3
FilePosition
src\eShopWCFService\Web.config

Explanation

System.Data.SqlClient dependency is detected.

While System.Data.SqlClient will work in Azure, the newer Microsoft.Data.SqlClient package is the primary .NET SQL client moving forward and receiving the latest features. For example, Microsoft.Data.SqlClient easily allows use of Azure Managed Identity from a connection string.

Explanation

Static content detected.

Your current approach of serving static content directly might lead to increased costs, performance issues, maintenance challenges (requiring application redeployment for content changes), and security risks.

Consider moving static content to Azure Blob Storage and adding Azure CDN.

WCF Client APIs
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

WCF client-side APIs for building service clients that communicate with WCF services. These APIs are available as exact equivalents via NuGet packages - add System.ServiceModel.* NuGet packages (System.ServiceModel.Http, System.ServiceModel.Primitives, System.ServiceModel.NetTcp, etc.)
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
GDI+ / System.Drawing
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

System.Drawing APIs for 2D graphics, imaging, and printing that are available via NuGet package System.Drawing.Common. Note: Not recommended for server scenarios due to Windows dependencies; consider cross-platform alternatives like SkiaSharp or ImageSharp for new code.
Windows Forms Legacy Controls
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy Windows Forms controls that have been removed from .NET Core/5+ including StatusBar, DataGrid, ContextMenu, MainMenu, MenuItem, and ToolBar. These controls were replaced by more modern alternatives. Use ToolStrip, MenuStrip, ContextMenuStrip, and DataGridView instead.
Windows Forms
 Mandatory 1
FilePosition

Explanation

Windows Forms APIs for building Windows desktop applications with traditional Forms-based UI that are available in .NET on Windows. Enable Windows Desktop support: Option 1 (Recommended): Target net9.0-windows; Option 2: Add <UseWindowsDesktop>true</UseWindowsDesktop>; Option 3 (Legacy): Use Microsoft.NET.Sdk.WindowsDesktop SDK.

Data Storage & External Services

One service owns a single EF context with five entity sets. Default storage is LocalDB eShopDatabase; the ConnectionString environment variable can replace that connection. No external HTTP API, queue, distributed cache, identity provider, or cloud integration is wired in the inspected scope. Pictures are local client assets, not streamed by the service. See data-architecture.md and configuration-inventory.md.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The desktop controller composes catalog and discount responses; there is no API gateway. Startup constructs dependencies manually rather than using a DI container (src\eShopWinForms\Program.cs:22-26, src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:75-84).
  • The WCF service directly queries EF; no repository or separate business-service project exists. A constructor accepts an EntityModel, but default activation constructs it (src\eShopWCFService\CatalogService.svc.cs:16-25).
  • Contract artifacts are not fully synchronized: the generated client accepts nullable filter IDs while current server requires integers. Diagrams describe intended source wiring, not proof of wire compatibility (src\eShopWinForms\Connected Services\eShopServiceReference\Reference.cs:513-517, src\eShopWCFService\ICatalogService.cs:20).

The server's entity classes double as [DataContract] / [DataMember] DTOs; there is no gateway aggregation DTO or immutable contract type. See data-architecture.md for fields and relationships. SOAP XML serialization uses WCF data contracts, not the merely declared Json.NET dependency.

Generated/stale artifacts: the desktop explicitly compiles Connected Services\eShopServiceReference\Reference.cs (src\eShopWinForms\eShopWinForms.csproj:89-92), whose generated models support data binding. Its GetCatalogItems(int?, int?) differs from current server GetCatalogItems(int,int) (Reference.cs:513-517; server interface:20); collections become arrays on the generated client. Current controller passes concrete integers, but this does not establish compatibility for null callers or prove the WSDL is current. The .wsdl, four .xsd files and .svcmap are saved generation artifacts, not live observations (src\eShopWinForms\Connected Services\eShopServiceReference\Reference.svcmap:21-30). No OpenAPI, protobuf or GraphQL definition was found.

The handwritten src\eShopWCFService\CatalogServiceClient.cs:11-38 has unimplemented methods and an obsolete parameterless call; it is not included in the service project's explicit compile items (src\eShopWCFService\eShopWCFService.csproj:79-94). Do not treat it as the active desktop proxy.

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous: desktop controller invokes generated WCF client synchronously. Generated Task wrappers exist but are not used by these workflows (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:35-84; Reference.cs:501-559). No queue, event bus, callback or one-way messaging is wired.
  • Composition: the desktop obtains catalog items and the current discount separately and calculates display pricing. This is client composition within one service, not a gateway calling multiple domains.
  • Resilience: no application retry, circuit breaker, fallback, bulkhead or explicit binding timeout is configured. The empty named basicHttpBinding relies on WCF defaults; no timeout values are source-pinned (src\eShopWinForms\App.config:20-23). Errors propagate rather than returning a documented degraded response.
  • Addressing: fixed development HTTP service address; no service discovery or load-balancing component. Startup requires the service and database to work before the dialog appears; details in configuration-inventory.md.
  • Security: the active client and explicit service endpoint use HTTP/basicHttpBinding without configured authentication, transport security or application authorization checks. HTTPS protocol mapping and metadata flags are present but do not prove a TLS-protected active endpoint (src\eShopWCFService\Web.config:27-40). External IIS policy is unknown; this assessment does not claim actual Internet exposure. Exception details are disabled in SOAP faults.

Core Business Workflows

The application lets desktop users browse a merchandise catalog with promotional display prices, look up dated stock availability and record availability quantities. Although named eShop, the scoped implementation has no checkout, customer, payment, ordering or shipping execution workflow.

Evidence paths are relative to eShopLegacyNTier. Workflows describe actual source logic; successful execution and generated-client compatibility are not verified.

CatalogBrandCatalogService / CatalogBrand lookupCategorizes catalog items
CatalogTypeCatalogService / CatalogProduct-type lookupCategorizes catalog items
CatalogItemsStockCatalogService / AvailabilityAvailable quantity for an item on a particular dayLogical item reference; not a shipment lifecycle
DiscountItemCatalogService / PromotionsDate-bounded global display discountApplied by desktop to returned catalog; no per-item association

These are responsibilities within a single business service, not separately deployed bounded contexts. The desktop is not a gateway and there is no independent discount service. Evidence: src\eShopWCFService\EntityModel.cs:18-22; src\eShopWinForms\Program.cs:22-26.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Initialize and browse a filtered catalog

  1. Startup constructs the form, generated service client and controller, subscribes to view events and loads data before displaying the dialog (src\eShopWinForms\Program.cs:22-27; src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:14-20,150-157).
  2. Initialization checks for the current-day discount banner, loads initial catalog items, then brand/type selectors and the shipment/availability item selection list. These calls are sequential and synchronous.
  3. A brand/type selector change sends both selected IDs to the controller; it clears the grid, requests catalog items, then separately requests today's discount (src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:106-135; controller:27-30,75-84).
  4. The service applies the zero-means-all filter rule. The controller supplies zero discount when no promotion is returned. The view applies the display-price rule, loads local picture assets and adds grid rows (src\eShopWCFService\CatalogService.svc.cs:56-62; view:48-61).
  5. There is no server-side persisted repricing, cart or order. Service/image failures are not caught by this workflow; the grid has already been cleared on filter refresh.

Banner content is calculated separately from catalog rendering, and is checked during LoadView rather than on every filter change (CatalogController.cs:60-69,150-157). This can produce a stale banner if the process remains open across a date change; it is not a background promotion refresh.

Workflow 2: Record an item's dated availability

  1. User selects an item and supplies quantity and arrival-date text. The view applies the availability input guard and parses values (src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:157-167).
  2. Controller creates a stock contract and calls CreateAvailableStock (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:35-43).
  3. Service finds the first stock entry for the same item and calendar date. Under the replace-not-increment rule, it overwrites an existing quantity; otherwise it uses the manual ID allocation rule, adds a row and saves (src\eShopWCFService\CatalogService.svc.cs:99-117).
  4. Only after a successful synchronous return does the view show a confirmation and clear inputs (src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:189-195). Failure has no implemented retry, compensation or friendly fallback.

The UI says "Shipment", but there is no shipment entity, carrier interaction, stock accumulation, reservation or inventory decrement process. Repeated entry for the same item/day replaces the stored amount rather than adding a delivered quantity.

Workflow 3: Look up dated stock

  1. User selects an item from the list and a calendar date. The view parses the selected item's ID; the selection parsing limitation applies (src\eShopWinForms\Views\CatalogView.cs:142-151).
  2. Controller requests availability. Service selects the first row matching item and date, returning its quantity or zero (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:50-54; src\eShopWCFService\CatalogService.svc.cs:90-96).
  3. View appends a result row containing date, item and quantity. It does not aggregate across dates or calculate running stock (CatalogView.cs:173-182).

Workflow 4: Establish initial catalog state

On first database creation, the initializer adds catalog types, brands, products, availability and promotions using factory data, saving each group separately (src\eShopWCFService\Models\Infrastructure\CatalogDBInitializer.cs:11-79). All stock/promotion sample dates are in 2017 (PreconfiguredData.cs:41-50,65-74 in the same directory). A newly initialized database therefore does not automatically have a currently active discount.

Other exposed operations

Find/create/update/remove catalog operations are in the service contract and implementation, but the inspected desktop controller does not wire catalog CRUD buttons or invoke those operations (src\eShopWCFService\ICatalogService.cs:15-34; src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:14-157). Their presence is an API capability, not evidence of a complete end-user maintenance workflow.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There is one remote business-service boundary: desktop → CatalogService. Catalog/brand/type/availability/discount operations all use that service and database. Catalog display composes two responses in the desktop: catalog items plus a separately fetched promotion; a null promotion becomes an undiscounted display. This is not circuit-breaker degradation, and an unavailable promotion request does not fall back to an undiscounted catalog—the exception propagates (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:75-84).

There is no queue choreography, cross-service saga, remote join by bulk IDs, API gateway or asynchronous event processor. No scheduled business entry point was found in scoped source.

Generated client and saved schema accept nullable catalog filter IDs, while the current server contract requires integers and treats zero as no filter (src\eShopWinForms\Connected Services\eShopServiceReference\Reference.cs:513-517, CatalogService.xsd:31-35 in the same directory; src\eShopWCFService\ICatalogService.cs:20). Diagrams show the intended current call chain, not a proven interoperable deployed contract.

Key Repository Methods

There is no repository interface. CatalogService directly accesses DbSets; the table documents its data-access methods rather than inventing a repository abstraction.

No raw SQL, stored procedure calls, batch cross-service finder or explicit TransactionScope is present in these paths. EF provides its normal per-SaveChanges transaction behavior; there is no explicit transaction spanning the preliminary read and subsequent write. The remove path does not explicitly attach a detached SOAP entity before Remove, so successful remote deletion must not be assumed.

Caching Strategy

No configured application result cache, distributed cache, second-level EF cache, cache TTL or invalidation policy was found in the context, service or runtime configuration. EF change tracking inside a context is not a shared catalog cache. ToList materialization is not cache-aside caching. The compiled but unwired CatalogServiceMock holds seeded lists; it is a mock, not a caching provider (src\eShopWCFService\CatalogServiceMock.cs:13-23).

Data Ownership Boundaries

All persisted catalog, promotion and availability data belongs to the same service and context/database; this is not database-per-microservice or CQRS. The desktop's only traced data source is WCF; its EF package declaration does not establish direct shared-database access. Client-side composition combines catalog and discount results without an additional persisted read model (src\eShopWinForms\Controllers\CatalogController.cs:75-84).

Application-managed Max+1 keys are not protected by an explicit read/write transaction or concurrency token. No uniqueness annotation protects the logical item/date pair, and overlapping discount intervals are not constrained in the model. These are source-observed persistence limitations, not a claim that a production database has no additional controls.
